value.overview: The Pale-billed Woodpecker (Campephilus guatemalensis) is a large Neotropical woodpecker found from Mexico through Central America to western Panama. It is strongly associated with mature forests but also uses forest edges, dry woodland, mangroves, and scattered standing dead trees. Its striking pale bill, black plumage, white facial and neck markings, and red crest make it distinctive. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species occurring on both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, mainly in lowlands and foothills.
value.classification: The Pale-billed Woodpecker belongs to the woodpecker family Picidae and the genus Campephilus, which includes several large, powerful forest woodpeckers. Its Costa Rican populations are generally assigned to the nominate subspecies, Campephilus guatemalensis guatemalensis.
value.identification: This is a very large woodpecker with mainly black plumage, bold white lines along the face and neck, and a pale ivory-colored bill. The male has an extensive red crest and red on the rear crown, while the female has more black on the forehead and crown. The wings and back may show pale markings, and the underparts can appear subtly barred. Its deep, forceful double knocks and loud calls are useful clues in dense forest.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from eastern and western Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and western Panama. In Costa Rica it occurs on both the Pacific and Caribbean slopes, including lowland tropical forest, humid evergreen forest, seasonally dry forest, mangroves, and forest edges. It is most frequent in areas retaining mature trees and standing dead wood, but may visit more open sites to forage on suitable trunks. It reaches foothill and lower montane habitats, locally to about 1,400–1,500 meters.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally nonmigratory. Individuals maintain home ranges throughout the year, although they may move locally in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The Pale-billed Woodpecker excavates a deep nest cavity in a dead or partly dead tree, usually high in a trunk or large branch. Both sexes participate in excavation, incubation, and feeding the young. In Costa Rica, breeding activity has been reported mainly from August through September, though timing can vary locally. The nest typically contains about two eggs. Retaining large dead trees is important because suitable nesting sites are limited in heavily cleared or intensively managed landscapes.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on large insects and their larvae, especially wood-boring beetle larvae found beneath bark or inside decaying wood. Termites and other small insects are also eaten, and small fruits may supplement the diet. The bird usually forages on medium and large trunks and limbs in the middle and upper forest levels, using its powerful bill to strip bark and excavate rotten wood. It may also investigate stumps, fallen logs, and dry standing trees.
value.behavior: Pale-billed Woodpeckers are usually seen singly or in pairs and are strongly territorial. They climb trunks using stiff tail feathers for support and deliver deep, resonant knocks while communicating or excavating. Pairs may forage on the same tree while remaining several meters apart. They generally do not join mixed-species feeding flocks. Their large size, powerful movements, loud double knock, and preference for substantial trunks often reveal their presence before the bird is visible.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be at immediate risk, although detailed population estimates and long-term trends are limited, particularly in parts of Central America.
